pronunciation.approximation: nyoo-wah, low-dipping tone on Nǚ, high level on Wā.
pronunciation.note: Nǚwā 女娲 bears the third tone on nǚ — the vowel ü written with its two dots, which the restoration keeps and plain ASCII drops. Wā is the level-toned archaic graph for this goddess alone: a character invented for her name, used for nothing else in the language. The ü is the front rounded vowel — the sound French writes u — which plain ASCII loses to plain u.

domains.title: The Mender of Heaven
domains.subtitle: The Five-Colored Stones, the Clay, and the First People
domains.lead: Nǚwā is the great repairer: the goddess who melted five-colored stones to patch the broken sky, cut off the giant turtle's legs to prop the corners of the world, and — on a quieter day — knelt by the Yellow River and made the first human beings out of mud.

cards.name: The Five-Colored Stones
cards.desc: Melted and poured into the sky's wound — the world's first and greatest repair, one stone left over (the seed of Dream of the Red Chamber).

cards.name: The Serpent Body
cards.desc: Her form in Han art: human head, serpent body — earth's maker in earth's image, twined with Fúxī.

cards.name: The Rope of Mud
cards.desc: The rich she shaped by hand, the poor she flung from a rope — humanity's two fortunes, told without flinching.

cards.name: The Marriage Rites
cards.desc: She prayed to become the matchmaker and instituted marriage — society's first legislator, outsourcing creation to love.

symbols.name: The five colors
symbols.meaning: The five phases (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) — the sky rebuilt in cosmic order

symbols.name: The compass
symbols.meaning: Her emblem in Han art, paired with Fúxī's square — heaven's measure in her hand

symbols.name: The turtle's legs
symbols.meaning: The four pillars she cut and set — sacrifice repurposed as architecture

symbols.name: The rope of mud
symbols.meaning: Her tool of mass creation — and the myth's blunt explanation of why fortunes differ

symbols.name: The stone she did not use
symbols.meaning: The one stone left over after the mending — the stone that becomes the jade of Dream of the Red Chamber and the book itself

mythology.lead: Nǚwā's myths answer the two great questions — where people came from, and why the sky holds — and a third the tradition added later: what happens when the whole human race must begin again. They are told in the earliest strata of Chinese myth and never improved upon.

myths.title: The Mending of the Sky
myths.text: The Huáinánzǐ (ch. 6, the Lanming xun, c. 139 BCE) tells it in the grammar of catastrophe: in high antiquity the four pillars snapped and the nine provinces split; fire blazed unquenched, waters rose undrained; fierce beasts devoured the people and birds of prey seized the old and weak. Then Nǚwā acted, and the text lists her works like an engineer's report: she smelted stones of five colors to patch the azure sky; cut the legs from the great turtle to set the four pillars true; slew the black dragon to deliver Jì province; and heaped reed-ashes to dam the flooding waters. Then — and only then — 'the people of the four quarters could set foot on the land again', and the cunning beasts went quiet. Nothing in the passage is creation from nothing: heaven is mended with worked matter, propped with sacrifice, and drained with humble ash. The oldest Chinese creation story is a repair manual, and its author is a goddess with a craftsman's hands.

myths.title: People of Yellow Earth
myths.text: The gentler myth survives in quotation from Ying Shao's Fengsu Tongyi (c. 195 CE): when sky and earth had opened and there were not yet people, Nǚwā knelt by the Yellow River and shaped human beings from yellow clay. The work delighted but wearied her — so she trailed a rope through the mud and flung the drops loose, and the drops too became people. The handmade figures became the rich and noble; the rope-flung drops, the poor and common — China's oldest surviving reflection on how inequality began, set inside its tenderest creation story. Note what the myth refuses to do: it does not blame the poor for their fortune or flatter the rich for theirs. Both were made by the same hands in the same afternoon; the difference is only which instrument touched them. Two thousand years before the word existed, the tradition was teaching that class is an accident of the tool.

myths.title: The First Matchmaker
myths.text: Having made people singly, she made them continuous. The Fengsu Tongyi continues: Nǚwā prayed at the shrine of the go-between, asking to become the divine matchmaker (Gāoméi), and so established marriage and its rites — so that humanity could reproduce itself without her kneeling by the river forever. The tradition therefore names her among the Three August Ones: progenitor, legislator, and engineer in one. Her strangest attestation is older still: the Shan Hai Jing ('Dahuang xijing') names ten spirits who dwell in the wilderness of Lìguǎng and calls them 'the intestines of Nǚwā, transformed into gods' — a fragment so archaic that the commentators have debated it for two millennia. Marriage and statecraft, clay and catastrophe, and one unglossable line about what a goddess leaves behind in the world: the sources give us a figure complete and still, after all this time, unexplained.

myths.title: The Two Survivors of Mount Kunlun
myths.text: The tradition's later stratum sends the flood. When the waters drowned the world, only Fúxī and Nǚwā remained, brother and sister sheltering on Mount Kunlun — and the human race hung on their decision. They wished to marry and continue the line, but hesitated: were they not siblings? So they put the question to heaven itself. The fullest surviving version comes down through quotation from the Tang collection Duyi zhi (Li Rong, 9th century): each climbed a separate peak and kindled a fire, resolving that if the two smokes joined as one, the marriage was approved. The smokes mingled in the sky. They married, and Nǚwā bore — not children but a ball of flesh; ashamed, she cut it into pieces and scattered them, and the pieces became the peoples of the world. The myth is startling for its honesty: heaven's consent is asked, the body is divided to make the nations, and the founding marriage of humanity is a marriage that had to be permitted. Even the gods, it says, do not waive the need to ask.

lore.syncretism: She pairs with Fúxī as sister-wife in the Han synthesis — their intertwined serpent bodies, compass and square in hand, form the canonical image of cosmic order on tomb stones from Shandong to Sichuan — and she absorbs older creation figures as the myth spread south and north. Daoist tradition adopted her without difficulty: a goddess who mends heaven and authorizes marriage fits a canon of celestial bureaucracy. Modern readers note her kinship with every world-mother from Gaia to the Navajo Changing Woman, but the Chinese tradition keeps her distinct signature: she is not just a mother but a repairer, the goddess of maintenance. And the novel Dream of the Red Chamber completed her canonization in literature, making the one stone she rejected for the sky the seed of China's greatest book.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her stones became literature: the great novel Dream of the Red Chamber (Hónglóu mèng) opens with the one stone Nǚwā rejected for the sky — the stone that becomes the hero's jade and the book itself. 'Nǚwā mends the sky' is the standing idiom for heroic repair; engineers, surgeons, and diplomats are all praised with it. Temples to her survive across North China — Shexian's cliff-hanging Wahuang Palace in Hebei is the grandest — where she is still prayed to for children. Her name entered the language twice over: as Wāhuáng, the August Wa, and in the everyday compliment of the mender of any broken thing.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Nǚwā is the goddess of the second day — the one after the catastrophe. Creation, in her myth, is not a single word but a continuous mending: sky patched, pillars reset, people shaped and taught. She asks the question every survivor, every parent, every civilization must answer: the world broke once; what, with your own two hands, have you repaired?

The rope and the handmade figures remain the tradition's quiet self-critique: some are shaped with care, some flung from a rope — and the goddess who made both is the one who mends the sky for all of them. Repair is her gospel and her rebuke: the world will break — pillars snap, heavens leak — and the measure of the maker is not the first creation but the mending. She is, for every restorer, nurse, and engineer of last resort, the patron of the second day.

lore.archaeology: The Wahuang Palace at Shexian — pavilions chained to a cliff above the Zhang River, founded in the Northern Qi dynasty (6th century) — is her principal surviving sanctuary and one of China's architectural marvels. Han pictorial stones pair her with Fúxī from Shandong to Sichuan; the Astana cemetery silk banner carried the image to the Silk Road's far end. Her myth's textual strata are mapped from the Huáinánzǐ (139 BCE) backward into Warring States fragments and forward into the Tang flood-cycle accounts.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 女娲: nǚ (woman) plus wā — a graph so specific to her that dictionaries list almost no other word under it. The ü of the restoration is the sound itself; without it, the name is another word.
